Pregnancy

Could it be twins? Early symptoms and how to find out

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Stronger pregnancy symptoms can make you wonder whether you are carrying more than one baby. Some people suspect twins before a scan; others have no particular clues and are surprised by the result. Symptoms and hormone tests can raise questions, but an ultrasound is the reliable way to establish how many babies are developing.

Symptoms are clues, not a way to count babies

Twin and singleton pregnancies share many early symptoms. Fatigue, nausea, breast changes and needing to urinate more often can occur in either. Their intensity varies considerably between people and even between pregnancies in the same person.

Having several strong symptoms does not add up to a diagnosis of twins, and mild symptoms do not rule twins out. A feeling that this pregnancy is different is worth mentioning at an appointment, but it cannot replace imaging. Arrange routine prenatal care rather than waiting for a distinctive symptom to appear.

Nausea and vomiting may be more noticeable

Pregnancy sickness often begins in the early weeks and can occur at any time of day. It is more likely with a multiple pregnancy, but many people carrying one baby also have substantial nausea or vomiting. Hormonal factors contribute; symptom severity is not simply a measure of the number of babies.

Symptoms lasting beyond week 14 are not a dependable twin-pregnancy sign. Sickness can continue later in a singleton pregnancy too. Severe symptoms may be hyperemesis gravidarum and deserve assessment regardless of whether you have one baby or more.

Contact your maternity team promptly if you cannot drink enough, are losing weight or feel dehydrated or very unwell. Dark urine, marked thirst or drowsiness are reasons to seek advice. Do not assume you just need to tolerate severe vomiting because twins might be present.

Tiredness is common in both kinds of pregnancy

You may feel exhausted around the time of a missed period or during the weeks that follow. Hormonal changes, disrupted sleep and repeated bathroom trips can all make rest more difficult. Some people expecting twins describe greater tiredness, but the feeling cannot identify a multiple pregnancy.

Make room for rest where possible, whether that means an earlier bedtime, accepting practical help or taking a break during the day. Discuss tiredness that is severe, persistent or interfering with normal activity with your clinician. There may be reasons to assess your health beyond the question of twins.

What a high hCG result can tell you

Human chorionic gonadotropin, abbreviated hCG, is the pregnancy hormone detected by urine tests. A quantitative blood test measures its concentration. A home test generally tells you whether enough hormone is present for a positive result; the darkness of its line is not a reliable way to count babies.

Higher hCG may occur with twins or triplets, but there are other explanations, including being further along than expected. Values vary widely. There is no single result that confirms twins or proves that a pregnancy is developing normally.

A clinician may order repeat measurements for a particular reason, including after fertility treatment or when assessing early-pregnancy concerns. Interpretation uses the starting value, change over time, dates, symptoms and ultrasound findings. A rigid rule that every healthy result must exactly double is not an appropriate home diagnostic test.

Hearing two sounds does not confirm two babies

If a clinician thinks they hear more than one fetal heartbeat, they can arrange or review an ultrasound to clarify the finding. Listening alone is not a dependable way to establish a twin pregnancy.

Do not rely on a home Doppler to diagnose twins or reassure yourself that the pregnancy is well. The timing and interpretation of sounds vary, and hearing something does not replace a clinical assessment. A claim that twins can reliably be identified with a handheld Doppler at eight to ten weeks is too definite.

The useful question is what the scan shows: separate embryos or fetuses, their cardiac activity when visible, and their placental and sac arrangements. If an early scan cannot answer everything, your team will explain whether a repeat examination is needed.

Bump size and early movement are not proof

A bump that becomes noticeable early can prompt speculation, but abdominal appearance depends on more than the number of babies. Previous pregnancies, body shape and other individual factors affect how you look. Measuring the uterus is a clinical observation, not an early home twin test.

Movements are also unreliable for counting babies. They are generally first noticed between 16 and 24 weeks, sometimes later within that range in a first pregnancy. Feeling flutters early, or movement in several places, does not establish twins.

Once you are familiar with your baby’s or babies’ usual movements, contact the maternity unit immediately if they reduce, stop or change. Do not wait until tomorrow or use a Doppler for reassurance. If you have felt no movement by 24 weeks, tell your midwife.

How to understand weight changes with twins

Weight gain is not a diagnostic test for twins. Early gain can be modest, and nausea may mean little gain or some loss. An unexpected change should be discussed in context rather than compared with a single first-trimester target.

For a confirmed twin pregnancy, the CDC lists the following total pregnancy gain ranges according to BMI before pregnancy. These are planning references, not targets to achieve quickly or instructions to change your intake without advice.

BMI below 18.5: 50–62 lb, approximately 22.7–28.1 kg. This particular underweight-twin range comes from a different evidence source from the Institute of Medicine ranges below, as the CDC notes.

BMI 18.5–24.9: 37–54 lb, approximately 16.8–24.5 kg. BMI 25.0–29.9: 31–50 lb, approximately 14.1–22.7 kg. BMI 30.0–39.9: 25–42 lb, approximately 11.3–19.1 kg.

The cited table does not give a separate range for BMI 40 or above. Triplets or more also need individual advice. Your clinician can help interpret weight changes alongside nutrition, symptoms and the babies’ growth; the table is not a reason to ignore persistent vomiting or weight loss.

When ultrasound can give an answer

An earlier scan may identify twins, especially when imaging is arranged after fertility treatment or for a clinical concern. What can be seen depends on the stage of pregnancy and the examination. Very early findings may need follow-up rather than an immediate definite answer.

In NHS care, twins are usually identified at the scan around 12 weeks. The 11–14-week scan is especially useful for assessing whether the babies share a placenta or amniotic sac. If this is unclear, further assessment is needed. Other health systems may use different appointment schedules.

Do not assume that the anatomy scan at approximately 18–22 weeks should be the first opportunity to discuss suspected twins. Establishing the type of multiple pregnancy earlier helps the team plan appropriate monitoring. Ask what your next scan is intended to check and whether its findings are conclusive.

How likely is a twin pregnancy?

The chance depends on factors such as age, a family tendency toward non-identical twins and fertility treatment. These factors change probability; they do not tell you the result of an individual pregnancy. A treatment clinic can explain how its particular approach affects the chance of multiples.

Identical twins arise when one fertilised egg develops into two embryos; non-identical twins arise from two separately fertilised eggs. Family history is more relevant to the tendency toward non-identical twins than to identical twinning.

For context, CDC final U.S. birth data for 2024 report 30.1 twin live births per 1,000 live births. This statistic counts babies, not the proportion of pregnancies that are twin pregnancies. It is also a country- and year-specific population measure, not your personal chance of conceiving twins.

What changes after twins are confirmed?

A twin pregnancy usually needs additional antenatal appointments and scans. Whether the babies share a placenta or a sac is important because it affects the monitoring plan. The ultrasound report helps your care team decide what follow-up is appropriate.

Most people with a multiple pregnancy have healthy babies, but complications such as preterm birth and pre-eclampsia are more common. A team experienced in multiple pregnancy can explain those risks without assuming that a complication will occur.

Bring questions about symptoms, nutrition and practical support to your appointments. You do not need to be certain about twins before asking for help with sickness or exhaustion. The next useful step is an appropriate clinical assessment, rather than repeatedly comparing your symptoms with someone else’s.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ultrasound confirms the number of developing babies; symptom intensity, a home test and a Doppler do not.

Assess placental and amniotic-sac arrangements early because they guide twin-pregnancy monitoring.

Severe vomiting or reduced fetal movement needs assessment regardless of the number of babies.

Twin weight-gain references depend on pre-pregnancy BMI and need individual interpretation.

How BeMama can help

Write down your pregnancy dates, any fertility treatment and the symptoms you want help with. At the scan, ask how many babies are visible, whether placental and sac arrangements are clear, and when the next assessment is due.

When to seek help

Get prompt maternity advice if you cannot drink enough, are losing weight or feel dehydrated. Later in pregnancy, reduced, absent or changed movements require an immediate call to your maternity unit; a home Doppler cannot rule out a problem.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Twins can cause stronger symptoms, but symptoms alone cannot confirm or exclude them.
  • A high hCG result needs clinical interpretation and does not count babies.
  • An early scan also checks placental and sac arrangements, which affect care.
  • Weight and movement patterns are not dependable twin tests.
  • Ask for help with severe sickness or other concerns rather than waiting for confirmation.

Frequently asked questions

Does extreme tiredness mean I am having twins?

No. Fatigue can be marked with one baby as well as twins. Rest when possible and discuss severe or persistent tiredness with your clinician.

Does a high beta-hCG number prove twins?

No. Multiple pregnancy is one possible explanation, but dates and other factors matter. Repeat tests may help assess a clinical concern; ultrasound establishes the number of babies.

What is the most reliable sign of twins?

A clinically interpreted ultrasound showing more than one developing baby. Symptoms and suspected extra heart sounds may prompt a scan but cannot confirm twins.

When can I find out?

Some early scans identify twins. They are commonly confirmed at the first-trimester scan, around 12 weeks in NHS care. Placental and sac arrangements should also be assessed; unclear findings may need a repeat scan.

Do nausea after week 14 or early kicks mean twins?

Neither is reliable. Nausea can continue in a singleton pregnancy, and the timing of first perceived movements varies. Seek care for significant symptoms rather than using them to count babies.

What are my chances of having twins?

Age, family history of non-identical twins and fertility treatment can influence the chance. Population birth statistics are not an individual prediction; your clinician can discuss factors relevant to you.

Should I aim for the same weight gain as someone with one baby?

Confirmed twin pregnancies have different reference ranges, but an appropriate plan also depends on pre-pregnancy BMI and health. Ask your care team rather than selecting a target from symptoms alone.

Can I use a home Doppler while waiting for a scan?

It cannot reliably diagnose twins or assess the babies’ wellbeing. Contact maternity services about concerning symptoms or reduced movement, even if you think you can hear a heartbeat.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
